claude.sample_unit: Medicare inpatients (670 with sepsis, 19,565 controls) at one academic health system
models_evaluated: Shashikumar et al sepsis prediction model (AUC 0.82, 0.87, 0.9)

links.outcome: Excess sepsis cost savings from cost-optimized thresholds versus fixed 80% sensitivity threshold
links.effect: Optimized uniform threshold saved US $4.3B vs US $3.9B for uniform 80% sensitivity; heterogeneous optimized thresholds saved US $4.6B, almost US $700M more than the 80% standard.
links.quote: At the pair where the highest savings are achieved, heterogeneous thresholds can save over US $300 million relative to uniform thresholds (US $4.3 billion cost savings with uniform and US $4.6 billion with heterogeneous) and almost US $700 million compared to the 80% standard.

links.outcome: Cost savings and DOR when alert cutoffs are chosen accounting for false alarm tolerance and department incidence
links.effect: Department-specific optimized thresholds raised DOR by up to 50 versus uniform recommended threshold (DOR up to 116) and increased savings; simulated only, no clinician input tested.
links.quote: Figure 5 D shows that DOR can increase by as much as 50 when switching from a uniform recommended threshold to heterogeneous thresholds, even though DOR is not directly maximized.

links.outcome: Cost savings from tuning classification thresholds by diagnostic category for out-of-the-box models
links.effect: Heterogeneous thresholds gave gains highest for lower-accuracy models: US $3.7B vs US $3B with uniform at AUC 0.82; overall savings up to 12.3% from customized thresholds.
links.quote: Figure 4 C shows that the gains from choosing heterogenous thresholds by MDCs are the highest for lower-accuracy models.

unlisted_practices: Optimizing model thresholds by diagnostic category to minimize national excess costs
Improving clinician adherence to sepsis alerts to increase cost savings (simulated up to US $1B)

links.outcome: annual cost savings and diagnostic odds ratio
links.effect: Heterogeneous thresholds increased annual cost savings by almost US $700 million versus 80% uniform thresholds and US $300 million versus uniform chosen thresholds, while increasing diagnostic odds ratio by up to 50 at AUC=0.9 and α=20.
links.quote: Figure 4 D shows that heterogenous thresholds would increase cost savings by almost US $700 million each year, relative to 80% uniform thresholds and by as much as US $300 million each year, relative to a uniform chosen threshold.
